Opening

GROW · SCIENCE · Autumn 2 · Week 5 · LESSON A · 2 MINUTES

Science Connections: Evidence Control

Learning objective

I can match a science question to relevant evidence, explain the link and improve one answer without overstating it.

Success looks like

  • Select evidence that answers the actual question.
  • Link a claim to an observation and a science reason.
  • Keep a first response, then make one meaningful improvement.

The evidence desk contains force, space and climate cases. Choose the right evidence before you explain.

Two separate lessons

A · Explore and explain · 40 minutes

B · Answer Lab: Say It, Support It, Improve It · 40 minutes

Stop after Lesson A. Lesson B has its own start and exit.

Point, speak, sign, move cards, draw, write or direct an adult. Choose one route; equivalent science evidence does not require a written conversion.

Arrival

GROW · SCIENCE · Autumn 2 · Week 5 · LESSON A · 5 MINUTES

Four clues to start

Choose a route. Today’s responses decide the help you use. No previous worksheet is needed.

Supported · 4 questions

1. Match a reason

Which idea explains day and night: rotation or friction?

Help beside the question
Point, choose or say. Think of a location moving into light.

Answer guidance

Answer: Rotation.

2. Read a unit

A rover travelled 46 cm. Which part is the unit?

Help beside the question
Point, choose or say. The unit names how distance is measured.

Answer guidance

Answer: cm / centimetres.

3. Climate timespan

Should a climate claim use one afternoon or long-term patterns?

Help beside the question
Point, choose or say. Match the timespan.

Answer guidance

Answer: Long-term patterns.

4. Evidence or guess

Choose evidence: “I like smooth” or “smooth trials were 46, 44 and 45 cm”.

Help beside the question
Point, choose or say. Evidence is an observation or data, not a preference.

Answer guidance

Answer: The three recorded distances.

2. Read a unit

Answer: They reveal variation and whether a pattern repeats.

GROW · SCIENCE · Autumn 2 · Week 5 · LESSON A · 7 MINUTES

Watch, predict, explain

Predict, model, explain

My answer is ___. Evidence ___ supports it because ___. This does not show ___.

Make a prediction. Change one view, then use a label to explain what you notice.

Choose the question before choosing a science word. Not every correct fact is relevant.

Worked explanation · reveal after thinking

The 46/44/45 cm and 18/20/19 cm values are invented practice data, distinct from the later rover investigation. A wheeled object involves contact resistance; do not teach that rougher always means more friction in every situation. A globe models rotation, not precise sunrise times. Climate concerns long-term patterns.

Local explainer · 32 seconds · silent with captions

Use instead of part of the demonstration. It never autoplays and needs no internet.

Full text / no-video alternative

00–08 seconds · Question first
Choose the question before choosing a science word. Not every correct fact is relevant.

08–16 seconds · Find usable evidence
These invented repeated distances compare one surface test, not every possible surface.

16–24 seconds · Link the reason
For day and night, use rotation and lit/unlit observations—not a friction explanation.

24–32 seconds · Improve with a limit
Add an evidence value, a causal link or a limitation. Keep the first answer to show the change.

Choose a card first. No cards have been placed.

Read the card clues

Distance repeats: Smooth: 46, 44, 45 cm. Fabric: 18, 20, 19 cm. Invented practice data.

Contact resistance: In a controlled setup, resistance at contacts can affect how far the rover travels.

Fixed light: LEFT marker faces light; RIGHT marker faces away.

Rotating Earth: A place turns into and out of sunlight.

Extra carbon dioxide: More greenhouse gas can initially reduce net infrared energy loss.

Long-term temperature: Climate patterns are assessed over many years, not one cold morning.

Would a small change help? · optional

You may ask for a clearer diagram, fewer cards at once, reading help or more thinking time. Tell your teacher, ask privately, point or pass. Your teacher will say what can change and check whether it helped. No extra sheet is needed.

Group explanations · reveal after sorting

Distance repeats: Surface-distance question. Smooth: 46, 44, 45 cm. Fabric: 18, 20, 19 cm. Invented practice data.

Contact resistance: Surface-distance question. In a controlled setup, resistance at contacts can affect how far the rover travels.

Fixed light: Day/night question. LEFT marker faces light; RIGHT marker faces away.

Rotating Earth: Day/night question. A place turns into and out of sunlight.

Extra carbon dioxide: Warming question. More greenhouse gas can initially reduce net infrared energy loss.

Long-term temperature: Warming question. Climate patterns are assessed over many years, not one cold morning.

You do

GROW · SCIENCE · Autumn 2 · Week 5 · LESSON A · 10 MINUTES

Use the evidence yourself

Supported · use one response mode

1. Select

Match one evidence card to each of the three question labels.

Help: Surface / space / climate.

2. Explain

Complete one frame using a card and because.

Help: Say or point; an adult may scribe.

3. Bound the claim

Add “in this model” or “in this test”.

Help: Avoid always.

Standard · use one response mode

1. Select

Choose relevant evidence for three questions; reject one mismatch.

Help: Match the measured quantity or observation.

2. Explain

Build one answer with a claim, evidence and reason.

Help: Use a number with cm or a position label.

3. Bound the claim

State what the chosen evidence cannot establish.

Help: Only two surfaces and one rover were compared.

Stretch · use one response mode

1. Select

Justify each choice and explain why a plausible distractor is irrelevant.

Help: A true statement may still be irrelevant.

2. Explain

Build two linked answers with accurate vocabulary and meaningful limits.

Help: Keep a process separate from an observation.

3. Bound the claim

Explain what additional evidence would strengthen one claim.

Help: More repeats or additional setups have different purposes.

Use the application model · an alternative to writing

Choose the explanatory link

Use the digital choices or the matching paper page. One response mode is enough.

Gather and use evidence

No practical equipment is required: the evidence cards and supplied data are complete. Use a pencil, cards or typed answers. An adult may read, scribe or move cards at the pupil’s direction; use one response mode.

4 min · Match a question to a relevant clue.

2 min · A partner or adult asks “Which clue supports that?”
6 min · Keep the first response; add one accurate link or limitation.

Worked explanation · reveal after thinking

Surface: smooth gives longer travel in these practice data (44–46 versus 18–20 cm); less resistance is a plausible explanation under controlled conditions, not a universal rule. Day/night: a location rotates towards/away from light. Climate: extra greenhouse gases alter net energy loss; one cold day is not a global trend.

Improve the science, not the amount of writing

Retain the first response. Add the missing unit, replace an irrelevant reason or narrow an “always” claim to this test/model.

Point, speak, sign, move a card, draw or write. One useful change is enough.

Supported · 2 questions

1. Full explanation

Use one value or observation in a complete science answer.

Help beside the question
Point, choose or say. Answer → evidence → because.

Answer guidance

Answer: Example: smooth gave longer travel here, with 44–46 cm versus 18–20 cm, consistent with less contact resistance in this setup.

2. Keep it bounded

Choose “in this test” or “in every test anywhere”.

Help beside the question
Only this setup was compared.

Answer guidance

Answer: In this test.

Standard · 2 questions

1. Full explanation

Use one value or observation in a complete science answer.

Help beside the question
Answer → evidence → because.

Answer guidance

Answer: Example: smooth gave longer travel here, with 44–46 cm versus 18–20 cm, consistent with less contact resistance in this setup.

2. Keep it bounded

Repair “smooth surfaces always make every rover go farther”.

Help beside the question
Limit the conclusion to the test.

Answer guidance

Answer: In this test, this rover travelled farther on the tested smooth surface.

Use one value or observation in a complete science answer.

Use an accurate science word. Answer → evidence → because.

Use an accurate science word. Limit the conclusion to the test.

Knowledge organiser

GROW Science · Autumn 2 · Week 5 · Shared resource · Shared resource

Learning objective

I can match a science question to relevant evidence, explain the link and improve one answer without overstating it.

Key words

claim — the answer you propose

evidence — observations or data used to support a claim

reason — the science linking evidence to a claim

relevant — directly useful for this question

limit — what the evidence cannot establish

Remember

  • A correct fact is not always relevant to a question.
  • Use values and units, or a precise model observation.
  • Separate what you observed from why you think it happened.
  • An improved answer adds accurate science, not merely more words.

Success looks like

  • Select evidence that answers the actual question.
  • Link a claim to an observation and a science reason.
  • Keep a first response, then make one meaningful improvement.

My answer is ___. Evidence ___ supports it because ___. This does not show ___.

TA Brief

Current stage

Current stage:

Preparation and access

No practical equipment is required: the evidence cards and supplied data are complete. Use a pencil, cards or typed answers. An adult may read, scribe or move cards at the pupil’s direction; use one response mode.

Scientific care

The 46/44/45 cm and 18/20/19 cm values are invented practice data, distinct from the later rover investigation. A wheeled object involves contact resistance; do not teach that rougher always means more friction in every situation. A globe models rotation, not precise sunrise times. Climate concerns long-term patterns.

Responsive feedback within teaching

The lesson teacher hears an optional request, explains what can change, tries it and checks the effect. Passing or asking privately is valid. No compulsory participation task or new pupil form. Do not infer assessment codes from a click, download or written box.

1. Match a reason

Which idea explains day and night: rotation or friction?

Rotation.

2. Read a unit

Why is “46” alone weaker evidence than “46 cm”?

It does not specify the quantity or unit, so the meaning is unclear.

3. Climate timespan

Should a climate claim use one afternoon or long-term patterns?

Long-term patterns.

Why might three repeats be more informative than one distance?

They reveal variation and whether a pattern repeats.

Evidence cards

GROW Science · Autumn 2 · Week 5 · Shared resource · Shared resource

Read a clue, choose a group, then explain. Cut apart or point; no cutting is required.

Distance repeats

Smooth: 46, 44, 45 cm. Fabric: 18, 20, 19 cm. Invented practice data.

Contact resistance

In a controlled setup, resistance at contacts can affect how far the rover travels.

Fixed light

LEFT marker faces light; RIGHT marker faces away.

Rotating Earth

A place turns into and out of sunlight.

Extra carbon dioxide

More greenhouse gas can initially reduce net infrared energy loss.

Long-term temperature

Climate patterns are assessed over many years, not one cold morning.

Answers · A · Standard

GROW Science · Autumn 2 · Week 5 · Lesson A · Standard

Four-question arrival

1. Match a reason: Rotation.

2. Read a unit: cm / centimetres.

3. Climate timespan: Long-term patterns.

4. Evidence or guess: The three recorded distances.

Two-check exit

1. Evidence choice: Accept distance table for surface travel; fixed-light model for day/night; greenhouse-energy model for warming.

2. Link: Accept an explicit link, e.g. the table directly compares travel on the two tested surfaces.

MADE BY MATT / GROW SCIENCE

Staff · feedback and access

GROW Science · Autumn 2 · Week 5 · Shared resource · Shared resource

Audience and response

The lesson teacher is the named adult audience. Hear or read the pupil’s own science response. A click, downloaded file or completed box is not evidence that a request was heard.

Respond within the existing task

Offer reading help, fewer cards at once, clearer labels, an adult-directed model or additional thinking time. Say what can and cannot change, then check whether the adjustment helped.

No additional pupil artefact

A response can be spoken, pointed, signed, drawn or written. Do not require a separate Lundy record, signature or written conversion of an oral response.

An optional pupil-owned note such as “What I said, and what it changed” may be used in existing work. It is not a requirement. If scribing, keep the pupil’s own words; the adult is an audience, not a verifier.

Keep assessment honest

Use current school recording practice and unit criteria separately. This pack does not certify an award. Do not infer a policy code from automated checking or a download.
